documentation.range: As defined following the work of Card et al. (2016) this species occurs throughout most of South America, being absent only from Chile and Uruguay. Boa constrictor appears to be the appropriate name for populations from Trinidad and Tobago, although Trinidad is excluded from the range mapped by Card et al. (2016). The elevational range extends from sea level to about 2,000 m asl. The wide range encompasses different ecoregions, including Amazonia, Chaco, Pantanal, Cerrado, Caatinga, Atlantic Forest, Llanos, Chiquitania and Andean foothills. Following taxonomic changes the species is not considered to be native in the Caribbean (Henderson and Powell 2009). The species has been recorded from several Caribbean Islands but is not known to have established breeding populations and specimens collected are considered to be waifs (Powell and Henderson 2012). The species has been introduced to Puerto Rico (Powell and Henderson 2012).
documentation.population: This is a locally common species in both Trinidad and Tobago and South America. It was one of the most abundant species in a snake community at Espigão do Oeste, Rondonia, Brazil (Bernarde and Abe 2006), but was relatively rare in other regions, including cerrado savannas of  Estação Ecológica de Itirapina, SP (Sawaya et al. 2008). Across South America as a whole the species may be in decline, at an unknown but likely gradual rate.
documentation.habitats: This species occurs in a wide variety of habitats, including tropical and subtropical wet, moist, and dry forest, beaches, savannas, mangrove swamps, semi-arid scrub, gallery forest, wetlands, secondary growth and perianthropic areas (Strüssmann and Sazima 1993, Henderson et al. 1995, Carvalho and Nogueira 1998, Martins and Oliveira, 1998, Rodrigues 2003, Bernarde and Abe 2006, França and Araujo 2006, Leynaud et al. 2006, Loebmann and Haddad 2010, Nogueira et al. 2011).  Boas are active both during the day and night (Marques et al. 2016) and are semiarboreal, though adults are often found on the ground. It is a live-bearing species. Most accounts describe a seasonal reproductive cycle, with vitellogenesis in austral summer (January to February), but this varies by region and subspecies. Litter size varies between five and 41 neonates, and the gestation period is of four to six months (Pizzatto and Marques 2007). Males often aggregate around a single female during courtship (Bertona and Chiaraviglio 2003), and non-clonal but fatherless reproduction has been reported (Booth et al. 2011). Sexual maturity is not reached before the fourth year of age. Feeds on mammals, birds, snakes and lizards (Martins and Oliveira 1998, Bernarde and Abe 2006, França and Araujo 2006, Marques et al. 2016). It reaches 4,200 mm total length (Roze 1966, Henderson et al. 1995, Murphy 1997).
documentation.threats: The species is persecuted and harvested by humans for the skin and its meat, in some cases illegally (e.g. in Argentina - Giraudo et al. 2012) but these threats are generally localized and do not present a major threat to this species as a whole. This species is also affected by habitat loss due to oil, mining and agricultural activities in several parts of its range (e.g. Ecuador, Brazil, Peru, Argentina). It is not threatened on Trinidad and Tobago. At least  68% of the range in Brazil is still covered in original vegetation types, based on data from 2008. Habitat loss in concentrated in the southern portion of the range in Brazil, mainly in Atlantic Forest and Cerrado areas. The species seems to persist even is these densely occupied areas. The subspecies Boa constrictor ortoni has a very restricted range in southern Ecuador and northern Peru and it is being affected by habitat loss and human persecution (D. Cisneros-Heredia pers. comm. 2014).
documentation.measures: Currently, this species is of relatively low conservation concern and does not require significant additional protection or major management. Its range includes a number of protected areas throughout South America. It is listed in CITES Appendix II; the subspecies Boa constrictor occidentalis is listed in CITES Appendix I. A large amount of research on the ecology and conservation of Boa constrictor occidentalis in Argentina has been conducted by Chiaraviglio and colleagues (2006, 2007, 2011).  The subspecies is categorized as Amenazada in Argentina (Giraudo 2012).
documentation.use_trade: This snake is harvested for its skin and meat, and it is collected for the pet trade. Historically this species has been considered one of the most common boas (or even snakes overall) maintained in captivity (M. Auliya pers. comm. 2020); CITES trade data reports transactions of more than 97,000 live individuals in the period 2010–18, exported by range and non-range States. Among range states, the most prominent exporters (in terms of volumes) are Colombia (>43,000 specimens),  Guyana (> 3,100 specimens) and Suriname (>2,700 specimens). While Colombia mainly reported captive-bred sourced specimens, Suriname and Guyana predominantly exported wild individuals. Nicaragua, a non-range state, claims the export of >12,700 mainly captive-bred sourced specimens (https://trade.cites.org).
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its very wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category. The species is declining in some areas, but overall it is not threatened at present.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
Until recently, the widespread Boa constrictor was the only recognized species within the genus Boa, with multiple morphological variants across its range described as subspecies. Two Caribbean populations, described as Boa constrictor orophias and B. c. nebulosa, have been informally recognized as full species for almost a decade (Henderson and Powell 2009). Multiple recent studies (summarized in Card et al. 2016) have investigated the systematics of Boa constrictor across its wider range on both morphological and molecular grounds. The name Boa constrictor was subsequently confined to the South American clade defined by Reynolds et al. (2014), with North and Central American taxa referred to Boa imperator.

The systematics of Boa constrictor may require further research to resolve: Card et al. (2016) applied a model that made the a priori assumption that South American samples comprised a single species and so were unable to discriminate between South American clades. These authors did, however, report a sister relationship between a Colombian clade and the remainder of Boa constrictor + imperator based on mitochondrial data and also found support for three distinct mitochondrial clades within the remainder of B. constrictor. In their text these authors assigned records from the Choco of Colombia and Ecuador to B. imperator, apparently following the division between northern and southern clades first identified by Hynková et al. (2009), and suggested that the latter may range into Peru, but did not discuss the basis for this assignment their map of the three clades indicates a southern range limit for B. imperator in northernwestern Colombia.
